title: Where to put the stop
desc: Put the stop where the chart proves you wrong, then size to fit

cards.title: Where’s the stop?
cards.situation: The stock pulled back to a low of $47.20, then turned up. You buy at $50. Where should your stop go?

chart.label: Rally, pullback to a low of $47.20, then a turn up to $50

options.feedback: $49 is about comfort, not the chart. A normal wobble can hit it while your idea is still fine.

options.text: About $47, just below the pullback low
options.feedback: Below the low is where your idea is proven wrong. That’s where the stop belongs.

options.text: No stop: you’ll watch it closely
options.feedback: Watching isn’t a plan. Without a stop, one bad day can turn a small loss into a big one.

cards.work: Pullback low $47.20. Stop $47. If price breaks that low, the bounce has failed.

cards.title: A stop marks where you’re wrong
cards.text: Put the stop where the chart says the idea **has failed**: below the pullback low, or below a support zone. Not at a loss you can stomach.

chart.label: Entry at $50, stop at $47 just below the $47.20 pullback low

blocks.tip: Find the stop first. Then size the trade so that stop costs only 1%.

cards.title: Too tight vs. just right
cards.text: Same trade, two stops. Price dips to $48.30, then rallies.

chart.label: A dip to $48.30 hits a stop at $49.50
The same dip stays above a stop at $47

blocks.tip: Too far is wrong too: a $20 stop means tiny size and a target that’s hard to reach.

cards.foot: The tight stop was hit by a normal dip. The wider one, sized smaller, survived.

cards.title: Never move the stop further away
cards.text: When price nears your stop, it’s tempting to move it lower “to give it room”. That turns a planned small loss into a big one.

visual.label: Planned stop −$100, moved once −$250, moved twice −$400

cards.rule: the stop can move up to lock in gains. Never down.
cards.note: A stop isn’t a guarantee. If price gaps past it, you can lose more than planned.

cards.title: Place the stop
cards.q: Support runs from $79.50 to $80.50. You buy at $82 after a bounce off it. Where should your stop go?

options.feedback: $81.50 sits above the zone. A normal dip into support would stop you out.
Just below the whole zone. If price breaks $79.50, support has failed.
That’s far below the zone. It risks $17 a share, so your size would be tiny and the target hard to reach.
Without a stop, a break of support can run much further. Plan the exit before you enter.

cards.work: Zone bottom $79.50. Stop $79. Risk $82 − $79 = $3 a share.

cards.title: Too much risk?
cards.q: Your logical stop at $47 means $3 risk a share. That feels like a lot. What’s the right fix?

options.feedback: Moving the stop to $49 puts it inside the noise. Keep the stop where the idea fails and shrink the size.

options.text: Keep the stop, buy fewer shares
options.feedback: The stop stays where the idea fails. Fewer shares bring the dollar risk back to 1%.
No stop means no limit at all. Keep the stop and make the position smaller.

options.text: Buy more shares to make it worth it
options.feedback: More shares means more dollars at risk, not less. Shrink the size instead.

cards.headline: You can place a stop that makes sense.
lines: Stops go where the idea is proven wrong.
Below the pullback low or the support zone.
Too much risk? Fewer shares, not a tighter stop.
